title: Ephemeral Reserve Hypergraph and Fallback Playbook (PRD draft)
summary: Proposal for an ephemeral reserve orchestration model based on a hypergraph of tenant-to-reserve affinities, plus a fallback playbook that preserves latency SLOs while minimizing cost and noisy-neighbor impact.
problem_statement: Dedicated customers require predictable latency and isolation but also want burst capacity for spiky workloads. Current reserved-capacity patterns either overprovision (high cost) or rely on blunt prewarm pools that cause unfair noisy-neighbor behavior. We need an approach that: (1) lets tenants burst without violating isolation SLOs, (2) keeps cost close to committed capacity, and (3) degrades gracefully when capacity is scarce.
objectives: Deliver sub-2x cost overhead for common spike patterns vs pure reserved pools
Keep p99 latency within contracted SLOs for top-tier tenants during moderate bursts
Provide deterministic isolation guarantees for defined fences while allowing opportunistic sharing when safe
Enable controlled, observable fallback paths that application teams can opt into (quantized models, lower context fidelity, routed-hosted fallback)
out_of_scope: Full billing/contract redesign, client SDK changes, non-dedicated hosted-tier experiments (only integration hooks).
design_summary: Introduce an ephemeral-reserve hypergraph: nodes are (tenant, reserve-slot) affinities; hyperedges encode multi-tenant packing constraints and locality preferences. A coordinator runs a continuous optimizer that assigns ephemeral slots to tenants based on real-time demand signals, tenant priority, and historical cross-traffic affinity. When ephemeral reserves are insufficient, the coordinator triggers a prioritized fallback sequence (fidelity lane downgrade -> model variant fallback -> routed-hosted fallback) governed by tenant-configured degradation contracts.
architecture_notes: Components: demand signal collector (per-tenant qps, tail-latency, queue-depth histogram), hypergraph allocator (simulator-ready greedy+ML-guided solver), reserve pool manager (prewarm lifecycle), fidelity-lane manager (model variant catalog + quantization profiles), and fallback router. All components publish structured traces and metrics to Console for rollouts and A/B testing.
autoscale_policy_spec: Autoscaler runs on two horizons: short (30s–5m) reactive window using exponential smoothing of prefix demand and KV-cache warmness; medium (5m–2h) predictive window using workload fingerprinting and seasonality features. The allocator keeps a hedging buffer expressed as 'hedge credits' per tenant: credits are consumed during spikes and replenish slowly based on commit level and observed calm windows. Policy knobs: min_reserved_headroom_pct, max_hedge_credit_ratio, prewarm_lead_ms, reactive_decommit_grace_ms.
burst_strategies: 1) Ephemeral prewarm lanes: short-lived VMs/containers that can host tens of small inference shards. 2) Microcredit lending: high-priority tenants can borrow credits from low-activity tenants with soft consent and cost accounting. 3) Fidelity-adaptive bursting: temporarily switch to quantized model variant or shorter-context inference under contract. 4) Locality-aware packing: prefer same-rack ephemeral slots to reduce cold-start KV penalties.
isolation_controls: Isolation is enforced via a multi-layer scheme: hard fences (dedicated GPU pools pinned per-tenant), soft fences (ephemeral reserve hypergraph constraints that limit cross-tenant co-residency), and runtime throttles (p99-based circuit breakers). Tenants opt into isolation tiers in their contract: strict, balanced, or opportunistic. Strict tenants bypass microcredit lending and cannot be colocated with unknown peers in ephemeral lanes.
fallback_playbook: Fallback sequence (configurable per-tenant): 1) Graceful degrade (reduce max concurrency, tighten batching) -> 2) Fidelity lane switch (model variant/quantization) -> 3) Route to dedicated warm fallback reserved slot -> 4) Route to Redwood-hosted tier with transparent header indicating fallback reason. Each step emits a structured event and incrementally increases throttling if downstream capacity remains constrained.
simulation_and_validation: We will build a discrete-event simulator that ingests tenant fingerprint traces (qps distribution, burstiness index, locality tags) and evaluates cost vs latency outcomes for a candidate hypergraph topology. Success criteria: simulated p99 SLO violations reduced by 60% vs naive opportunistic pooling at <=1.8x cost of static reserved baseline for realistic spike mixes.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: internal A/B sims and operator-only feature gate (4 weeks). Phase 1: limited beta with 3 low-risk customers opt-in (prioritized balance tenants) and manual runbook (8–12 weeks). Phase 2: automated ops, expose tenant config and SLA terms in Console, expand to broad GA (quarterly). Each phase paired with targeted telemetry dashboards and rollback triggers.
metrics_and_alerts: Core metrics: tenant_p99_latency, ephemeral_slot_utilization, hedge_credit_balance, fallback_rate_by_tenant, cross_tenant_co_loc_violation_count, cost_per_inference_token. Alerts: spike in fallback_rate (>1% sustained), hedge_credit_exhaustion, sudden rise in cross_tenant_violation_count.
operational_runbook: - Detect: Console alert on fallback_rate. - Inspect: query traces for tenant id, slot id, hypergraph assignment. - Mitigate: temporarily raise headroom, disable microcredit lending for noisy tenant, or scale reserve pool manually. - Escalate: SRE on-call if p99 violations persist >10m or if rollback needed. Include playbook steps for customer comms template and SLA credit calculation.
security_and_compliance: Ephemeral lanes inherit tenant-level encryption keys; no KV cache is shared across hard fences. For regulated customers, restrict ephemeral assignment to single-tenant slots and ensure KMS keys never leave customer boundary. Audit logs record all fallback events and hypergraph reallocations.
open_questions: - Pricing: how to fairly bill microcredit lending and cross-tenant borrowing? - Long-tail cold start: is rack-locality enough to preserve KV warmness for large context models? - Solver complexity: can the allocator run in <200ms for typical cluster topologies? - Legal: what baseline SLA language is needed to allow routed-hosted fallback?
